neighborhoods_visited: Historic District - Forsyth to the River
guide_description: One day covering Savannah's historic core along the north-south spine from Forsyth Park through the moss-draped squares to the cotton warehouses on the Savannah River. The grid of 22 trust squares is the organizing logic of the city and this route threads the best of them in a single coherent walk.

days.cluster_tagline: Spanish moss, Federal-era squares, and cotton-trade architecture on the Savannah River
days.neighborhood_description: The largest National Historic Landmark District in the United States, covering 2.5 square miles of James Oglethorpe's 1733 grid. Twenty-two public squares punctuate the street plan at regular intervals, each originally a different ward with its own church, public buildings, and residential lots. The district runs from the wide boulevard of Forsyth Park in the south to the bluff overlooking the Savannah River in the north.

morning.notes: The 30-acre anchor at the south end of the historic district. The 1858 cast-iron fountain is the most photographed object in Savannah - approach it from the central north-south allée rather than from the Gaston Street gate, so the live oak canopy frames the reveal. Saturday farmers market occupies the perimeter from 9am; on other mornings the park is quiet enough to hear mockingbirds.

afternoon.notes: The Italianate mansion on Monterey Square built for General Hugh Mercer and completed in 1871, later owned by antiques dealer Jim Williams and made famous by John Berendt's Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil. The docent-led tour of the ground floor covers the architecture, Williams's art collection, and the trial without sensationalizing it. Tours run on the hour; the carriage house gift shop is run separately and does not require a ticket.

walk_to_next.to: Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist

evening.activity_title: Factors Walk and the Savannah Riverfront
evening.notes: The multi-level network of iron bridges and cobblestone ramps connecting Bay Street to the riverfront cotton warehouses below the bluff - cotton factors (brokers) worked these offices in the 19th century. The cobblestones on Riverfront Plaza are original ship ballast from European vessels. Walk the upper iron walkways along Factors Walk first for the warehouse roofline views, then descend to the river level for the sunset over the water.

if_time_permits.activity_title: Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist
if_time_permits.notes: The largest Catholic church in Georgia, rebuilt after an 1898 fire and completed in its current French Gothic form in 1900. The interior is worth the stop specifically for the stained-glass windows imported from Munich and the hand-laid mosaic tile floors - details that most visitors walk past quickly. Free to enter outside of Mass times.

One of the best-preserved squares on the north-south route, anchored by a 1910 bronze of James Oglethorpe facing south toward potential Spanish attack from Florida. The bench on the north side of the square was used as the filming location for the opening Forrest Gump scenes, though the actual bench is now in the Savannah History Museum - a fact the square's plaques do not mention.
